projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Jennifer Wassman was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: This is Charles Fuller interviewing Jennie Wassman on Dec. 30 at her home in Romeoville, Illinois. When were you born?

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Where were you born?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: In Columbia County, Wis.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: What was your hometown like?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Well, I was born on a farm, raised, and it was a little town. A little one-horse town, (laughs)

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: So it was a county? So they didn't have actual towns?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: No. They had actual towns, but I was born at home. And that was Cortland Township. Our county seat was Portage, Wis. Columbia County.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Do you remember how many people were in the town? I know you said it was a small town.

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: I really don't because I didn't pay that much attention to how many people, but.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Well, so, what did you guys farm?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: It was a dairy farm. In those days they had everything. Horses, cows, calves; everything.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: How far was the next farm from where you guys were? Did you even see your neighbors?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yes. You could see the neighbors. They were a little distance apart; maybe a quarter of a mile.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: How many children were in your family?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: (Laughs) We had 16, but one died when she was 11.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Where were you in that?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: I was the tenth child.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: This is sort of a weird question, but what kind of people were your parents? I mean, were they strict, were they religious? How did they really live their lives?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: They were Christians. We were Dutch so we carried a lot of the Dutch customs. They were good people. They were kind.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Were they strict?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: No. They weren't strict, but we had a routine. Mealtimes were. Meals were on time, bedtime was on time. We had a home like that. It wasn't chaos.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Were they first generation Americans, or were they born here?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: They were born in Holland, both of them, but they became American citizens.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: They moved here to make a living?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Well, they were both very young. My mother was 10 when she moved here, and my dad was 16. He came here to work. His uncles had a garden farm, and he came to work with his uncles.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Is a garden farm like for flowers?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: No. I think all kinds of vegetables and so on. They lived in Chicago on the South Side.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Your parents moved up to Wisconsin?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yeah, they moved up to Wisconsin when they got married. They met, and they got married, and they moved to Wisconsin. My mother had relatives here, in Wisconsin.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Where did you expect to be when you were younger? I mean, when you were younger, where did you expect to be when you were older?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Living in Wisconsin, (laughs) I thought I would be living in Wisconsin on a farm. I just never thought any further than that.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: What was your education as a child?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Eighth grade. Eighth grade was my education.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Was that normal?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: No. A lot of people went on to high school, but I didn't.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Because you were working on the farm?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: I just didn't go. I didn't want to go, and I didn't go. I didn't need to.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: So, did you have jobs outside of the farm, or was your only work to work on the farm with your parents?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Well, later on they moved away from the farm, and my dad did garden farming until the war began. Then he worked in a war plant.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: World War II obviously, right?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yeah. And then I would do housework, babysitting. Things like that. [Jennifer signals to stop the tape as she gets up to take care of something. When she comes back, the taping resumes]

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: What do you remember about the start of World War II?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: I remember the day that it happened; that it was announced. It was on Sunday.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: How did you get that kind of news?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Through the radio.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Was there even TV?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: No. No TV then. No. It was on the radio.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: What do you remember hearing about it? Just that it had started?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yeah. That we're in war now.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: How did it affect yourself, I guess, first, and then, how did affect the town you were in?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Well, of course the boys were drafted into the war. First, some went, and then as time went on, more got into it. And of course we were restricted from buying. Everything. All the factories were doing war stuff, making war products. You couldn't get anything. They didn't do any more cars, stoves, refrigerators. You just got along with what you had. Used cars.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: How many of the children were boys?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Nine.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Were they all drafted?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Oh no. No. Because some were married already. One was drafted. One went into the war.

sp.speaker: Peak
sp.p: Who?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Ben.

sp.speaker: Peak
sp.p: Was he drafted?

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: It's OK.

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yes. He was drafted, and he was already married. They had a child. But he didn't go overseas. He stayed in this country. After the war, two of my brothers went in. Post-war.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: When you heard stuff on the radio, was it sort of like, were they telling people to be worried? Was it nonchalant? How was it coming across? Like 'Oh, We're in War!' and were they making a big deal of it, or was it more relaxed?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Oh, I think so, they made a big deal out of it. My father, he kept his ear peeled to the radio, so he wouldn't miss anything. And the newspaper. But at that time, I really didn't pay much attention. I was at an age where I was thinking about having a good time, or. I wasn't worried about the war. Living with my parents, they handled everything.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: What did your parents say about the war? Did they talk about it?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Uh, oh yes. They often discussed it.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Discussed it between themselves?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yes. Well, everybody was war-minded in those days because we were in war.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: How close to the war did your dad leave the farm and get a job in a factory?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Well, we were living in a town then already. Uh huh. In a little town; Columbus, Wis. And he was doing garden farming. You couldn't buy tires anymore, and gas was rationed. Because he would go around selling his vegetables. So then he got a job in a war plant. A dry milk factory. They were making dry milk to send to the soldiers.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: So was that after the war had already started?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: What did you and your brothers and sisters say about the war when your parents weren't around?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Nothing special. It was just accepted amongst us. "So it is," and we lived with it. [Jennifer made a signal to stop the tape. She had to take a brief break.]

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: How. Did the reality of the war change during the course of it? Was there a point when the war seemed more real, or did it stay the same the whole time? I know it's a weird question. You know, some people say that war isn't really real until you know someone who died or something like that.

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: No. I think it seemed real.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Did you listen to the radio everyday about it?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Oh, my father did. Yeah. Uh-huh. (pause) Can I tell you about this?

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: OK. Well, what were your jobs during the war?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Uh, well first, while we still lived in Wisconsin, I worked in a dime store, different places, and I worked in a canning factory, where we canned peas and corn. And, it was seasonal. Times when the peas were ripe and the corn was ripe.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Was it peas and corn for people in America or for soldiers?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Uh.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Just whoever?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yeah. I think so.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Who did you work with there?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: While I was working there, we had prisoners of war---German soldiers. They were prisoners. They were camped out in a field nearby, and they brought them in to work in the factory because our men were all gone. The boys were all gone. I was doing jobs that would have normally been a man's job, but I could handle it. It wasn't that hard. So they had them working there. There were guards with guns surrounding them, watching. I couldn't talk to them because they couldn't speak English, and I couldn't speak German. But they were nice, young, handsome men. Mmm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Did they seem like they were riotous, or, you know, like they were mad or whatever for being captured?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: I think they were, but, uh. They weren't happy about it, but they had to behave because there were guards all around them.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: How else was women's role effected by all the men leaving? Was it just the changing roles in the workplace, or?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yes, because women started to take over a lot of the men's work, jobs.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: In everything?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Well, they were gone. More and more men went. I was a teenage girl at that time. That's when the song came out, "They're Either Too Young Or Too Old." The guys were all gone, and they were either too young or too old.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Did you feel like any of your civil liberties were affected by the war? [Jennifer doesn't understand.]

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Did you see anybody speaking out against the war? Was there anything like that going on?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: No, not so much I don't think as later on with the wars that came along. So, people accepted it, and they were very American. You know, for America. If you went to a show, or a dance or anything, at the end we had to sing "God Bless America."

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Uh-huh. Yeah. American songs. Everyone seemed very patriotic.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: How did you feel about that? Were you with them?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Oh sure.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: What did you know about the countries involved in the war? Did you know who was involved?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Well, we were fighting Japan and Germany. Uh-huh. Well, see, then I moved to Chicago. During World War II, my family moved to Chicago because I had a brother here, and he told my parents, "You should come to Chicago." Because there were quite a few of us living at home, and "they could all get jobs. Lots of work." They would come to the door and ask you if you could work even. So they did, and we did. And I worked in a factory that made trans, transformers. Winding coils.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: So you had to wind coils?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yeah, I wound coils. First I worked with hand winding, then I was on a machine where you did a whole bunch at once. You had to direct the wires.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Did those jobs pay well?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Well, we thought it was good because we really came out of the depression when the war started. Everybody was poor. They didn't have hardly anything. You worked hard for a dollar a day, and then we. Boy, I remember my first paycheck that was 27 dollars. I thought that was a lot of money.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Was that for two weeks or one week?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: One week.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Wow, so from one dollar a day to like four.

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: And they treated you very well at work. They were very good. They'd give you a break in the morning---coffee break---a break in the afternoon. They were very nice. Treated you good.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: So when you moved to Chicago, was it in the city of Chicago?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yes, in the city of Chicago.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: How close to where downtown is now?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Oh. Well, we could hop on a street car. They had street cars in those days. We could hop on a street car and go downtown. Twenty minutes. They didn't have malls then like Woodfield Mall (a large mall in Schaumburg, 111.) or all these malls. If you wanted to do any shopping you went downtown.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Like, to Michigan Avenue?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Well, and State Street, too. They had all the big stores; Carsons, Fields, [telephone rings] That was the only place you could find them in those days; downtown.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Do you need to answer that?

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: So what year.. .Do you remember what year you moved to Chicago?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: I think it was like 1944. Well, yeah, '44 or '45.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: OK, then you got the job winding coils, and how long did that last?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: I think until I got married. Then I met my husband.

sp.speaker: Peak
sp.p: That was Rachel. She wanted to know who's car was here.

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yeah, he had just got out of the service there when I met him. And I think the war had just ended. When did the war end? '45, '46?

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Yeah. Sometime around there. Sure.

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: And I met him, and I went with him for a year, and then we got married. That's when I quit. Then, the war was over.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: You took on a homemaker role?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Mmm-hmm. He was in the Navy, you know. In the South Pacific. For three years, he was on the little islands. Japan.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: And his name?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Don Wassman.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Um, what year did you meet him? Do you remember?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: I think it was '46.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: He was an electrician, right?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yeah. He was an electrician in the Navy, so when he got out, he got a job as an electrician.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Did he ever talk about his experience in the war?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Oh yes. A lot.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: What did he say?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: He was on a ship that carried troops that were, I think, that had been hurt. And they would take them where they had to go.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: So what did he say about it?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Oh, he told some horrible stories about how these people had been so badly injured.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Would they leave them on the boat until they were healthy enough to fight again?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: They took them, I think, to hospitals somewhere. Back to the States.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Do you feel like he had a positive or negative experience in the war?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Oh, positive. He was proud of his years in war. He experienced a lot, saw a lot. He was in the South Pacific. He went to islands...

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: He got to go around?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: ...Guam. He knew about all of them.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Did your brothers or sisters or close friends, did everybody have a war-related job? Did everybody get a job in a factory like you had?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Well, I had two sisters that were married who lived on farms. And I had some brothers in California. They worked on big dairy farms. Yeah, some of us worked in war plants.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: So the family had sort of separated a little at that point? You guys weren't all together?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: The older ones were all married.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Did the people who worked on farms, did they grow stuff for everybody? I know you said they didn't really make anything, but did farming stay the same?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yes. Feed for cows, and corn and peas for the pea factory, and milk, cream.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Do you remember any specific battle reports on the radio, like D-Day? [No response.] Or when they dropped the bomb?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Oh yes, I remember that. Sure. When they dropped that bomb on, uh, Hiroshima.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: What was that like?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: I guess I didn't realize how terribly bad it was. We didn't have television that would show you pictures like today. Only thing I knew was that the war was going to end, and that was good news. The war in Japan, that would end the war.

sp.speaker: Peak
sp.p: If you went to the movies, they showed pictures of the war.

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yeah, if you went to a movie, they would have news reels first. They would show you the latest news about what was going on in the war.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Do you remember Pearl Harbor? It was obviously before the bomb, but.

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yeah, that's when it happened.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: That's when we got involved, huh?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Was nobody really expecting that?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yeah. Nobody knew about it. No.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Were people talking about it?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: When did we go in war with Germany? Was the war in Europe going on when the Japanese war started?

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Oh, OK.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Yeah, and then the Japanese attacked us. Were you close with people who went to war? Besides your brother, like young men who became soldiers.

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Oh yes. Our friends. A lot of friends we had.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Did you correspond with them?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yes, I did.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: What were the letters like? What did they say? Good things?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: I can't remember.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Just sort of friendly letters?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Friendly letters, uh-huh. They didn't really talk about the war.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Did you see a lot of them when they came back? Came back from war, I mean?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Oh sure.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Did they seem the same?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: I guess, yeah, (laughs)

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: What kind of music were you listening to then?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Oh, the forties music. '45, you know.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Like swing music?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: I guess you would call that swing music. Not be-bop stuff like you have today. Rock 'n' roll wasn't even there then. That all came out later.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Was it big bands playing dance music?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. Laurence Welk, and all them. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Did everyone still go out and listen to bands while the war was going on?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yes. We used to go to the Aragon Ballroom, and they had big bands come and play there. Yeah. And we'd meet soldiers. They'd have time off, and we'd meet different ones different places.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Were they ever looking to talk about the war, or were they just hanging out?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: You know, I don't remember that.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Were there a lot of them when you went out, or only a few, and you'd see little groups?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yeah, little groups here and there. Soldiers and sailors.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Where did you meet Don?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: At a dance. A veterans dance. The war had just ended. It was a veterans dance.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: So he served till the end of the war? He served the last three years?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yeah, he stayed till the end.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: And you were looking to get married at that point?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: I suppose I was. (laughs) He was too.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: How did you feel about him being a war veteran?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: You just accepted that because that was the thing of the day.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: How do you remember hearing about the end of the war?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Oh my goodness. I went downtown, (laughs) Wrong thing to do. Everybody was excited. There was excitement all over. We got on a street car, some of my friends and I went downtown, and the people were just wild. They'd grab you and kiss you and they were throwing stuff around. It was awful.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Was that why you went downtown, or were you just going there anyway?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: We went because everybody. To celebrate. But it was wild. People were real excited.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: So it was a big announcement on the radio, that we had signed the treaty?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Oh yes. They would tell you the news where I was working. When Roosevelt died, they announced it.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: So were people like drinking and stuff? Kind of craziness?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: A stranger would grab you and hug you and kiss you. There were throwing stuff all over. I think we finally caught a street car and went home, got out of there. It was terrible, yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Was that a significant moment for you? Did it excite you?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Oh sure.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: But not quite enough to hang out with a bunch of people going crazy?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: No. (laughs)

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Were you religious during the time of the war?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Well, I went to church, but I had a lot to learn.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Did you feel like it was a positive thing for you during war? Helpful to go to church? Did the pastor talk about it?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: I can't hardly remember what the sermons. I, I didn't have a personal relationship with the Lord I don't think. I went to church, and I heard the stories, but they didn't. It was just. Not like I do now. I wish I had.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Did you notice a change in how everyone else, how the religion in everyone else changed during the war?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: No. It was just like it is now. People go to church.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Anything else about the war that particularly sticks out about the war?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Well, you couldn't get stockings during the war. They didn't even have nylons in those days. We'd paint our legs. Oh yeah, everybody did.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: What!? Did they have leg paint?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yeah. I talked to people. They all did the same thing. And, in those days, the stockings had a black seam up the back. Now we wouldn't wear them like that. So we'd even paint the black seam up the back of our legs. And you couldn't get shoes with leather soles. So they made wooden. So we had sandals with wooden soles. Clunked when you walked.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Because people were just working on war stuff?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yes. And you couldn't get sugar. You were rationed. So we stopped baking because you would just get enough for like your coffee and tea and things like that.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: How did they ration you?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Well, we had stamps. You had to go and register, and according to how many you had in your family, you'd got a book. But out of each you only got so much. And you couldn't buy meat. You had a lot of fish, and once in a while, you'd get some meat. We had to save all of our grease. There was a slogan: "Out of the fire," "Out of the frying pan, into the firing line." You saved your grease in a tin, and you brought it to the butcher when it got full. And they made ammunition out of that. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Do you know how they did that? I've never heard that.

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yeah. Remember that Peak, "Out of the frying pan, into the firing line"?

sp.speaker: Peak
sp.p: No, no. I was in California at the time.

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yeah, she was in California. So we'd save our grease, and we were rationed on sugar and, what else was it? And meat, meat.

sp.speaker: Peak
sp.p: Meat! And butter. You only had so many points a month.

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: So you could only get so much. That's why we stopped baking. Because we couldn't.

sp.speaker: Peak
sp.p: Everything went overseas.

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: To the soldiers, yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Did you have cars at that time?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yeah, but they were second-hand cars. You couldn't get tires much. Only old tires. Gas was rationed. You could only get so many gallons. You got used to living like that though.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: So when you moved to Chicago and your dad got a job in a factory, did your mom stay home all the time?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Because you had plenty of kids to take care of?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Well, in those days, women didn't work like they do now. When you got married, you stayed home, and you took care of your house and your children. They didn't have day care.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Was it frustrating for your mom to be rationed all this stuff?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: You learned to live with it. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: For the sake of the war effort?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: What lasting effects did the war have on you?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Nothing, I don't think. Except that you're more appreciative of your freedom. [Switch tape.]

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Do you think the war had any lasting effects on grandpa?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Don?

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: (pause) Let me think.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Did it teach him discipline? You didn't know him before the war to actually see the difference first-hand, but. [Jennifer has no response.] Did he ever wake up in the night, sweating, that kind of thing?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: No, no. He wasn't really in combat. He was on a ship.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Looking back on it now, from all the things you've seen, do you think it was right to go to war at that time?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Well, I guess they had to didn't they. Because the Japanese bombed us. Pearl Harbor. I don't know why we went to war with Germany. I don't even know why.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Well, Hitler was enslaving the Jews, although I don't really know how much we knew about that stuff.

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: We didn't. We didn't know about that till after the war.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Would you hear Hitler's name over the radio?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: When I was in grade school, the teacher told us about Hitler; he had his picture put on the stamps, he was raising these super-men. He was raising an army then, already. That was before the war. Yeah. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: So he was telling you about it in like history class? Or he was warning you about it?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Well, it was in the newspapers. So our teacher would tell us about it.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: So they knew about Hitler a long time before? That he was amassing these armies?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yeah. Mmm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: This is sort of a modern topic, too, but, war coverage, they talk about war coverage a lot now with the Iraqi war, rather, the war in Iraq. How did you feel? Did you feel like you were well informed? You probably weren't listening a ton to the radio, but

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: In those days?

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: We were informed. But, like I say, I was at an age where it didn't mean that much to me. My father did. He was very much. Gabriel Heater. Did you ever hear of Gabriel Heater?

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: He was a news commentator, and my father would sit with his ear in the radio so he wouldn't miss anything.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: How much of the radio was news? Was there news stations, or was it a music station that would break and then go to news?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: I suppose. It was just like it is now. We had news times, and if there was any big news report, it was interrupted on the radio. Sure. Just like now, on television.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Was it the same number of stations, or were there only two or three?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Oh, they didn't have FM then. It was only AM.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: But AM still played music?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yeah, sure. That's how we learned all our songs.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: They're either too old or too young.

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yeah, (laughs) "They're either too old or too grassy green." That's in that song. They were all war songs.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Do you think if you would have been a man, would you have been at war?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yes. In our family, us girls, there were four girls in a row, and we were the age, if we'd have been boys, we'd all have been drafted. But there were older boys and then younger boys. They were already married.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: So, if you were married, you didn't have to go to war?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: If you had some children, yeah, that would hold you back. Unless you wanted to.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Did a lot of people want to?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: There were a lot of 'em, yeah. They volunteered. Some were four-f s, and they couldn't get in. They felt bad. They had something wrong with them. They couldn't get in.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Did you ever feel afraid during time of war?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: No, not really. There was just no reason to.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Being at home, you didn't worry about bombs or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: No, we didn't have that in our country. Did we have blackouts, Peak?

sp.speaker: Peak
sp.p: I had 'em in California.

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: We did, I think, in Chicago, but I was living in Wisconsin.

sp.speaker: Peak
sp.p: You'd be riding on a bus, and all of a sudden it would stop and all the lights would go out.

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Do you know what a blackout is? Everyone had to turn their lights out. You couldn't have lights on.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: In case planes were flying over?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: But that never happened here?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Well, it did in Chicago, but I wasn't living here then.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: What smells and sounds bring you back to that time? Are there any? The music?

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: Yeah, the old songs they used to play. They were nice songs.

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Well, that's it.

sp.speaker: Jennifer Wassman
sp.p: That's all!

sp.speaker: Charles Fuller
sp.p: Thanks for helping me out.
